strengths: Addresses a genuine, practical problem: unsupervised selection among pre-trained segmentation models for microscopy, where no transferability estimator for instance segmentation exists and supervised estimators cannot be applied without target labels.
The proposed estimator is simple, computationally lightweight (only two inference runs), and applicable to both black-box and grey-box models, which is well matched to the model-zoo use case.

Evaluation spans multiple tasks (mitochondria EM, nuclei LM semantic and instance, cells instance) and many public datasets, with appropriate ranking metrics (Kendall tau, Spearman, Pearson) and comparison of feature vs. input perturbations.
The ablation on perturbation strength (Fig. 3) is informative, showing the ranking is robust across a wide range of dropout proportions.
Comparison against CCFV, a supervised state-of-the-art estimator, is a useful (if imperfect) reference point, and the paper candidly notes the apples-to-oranges nature of the comparison.
Clear problem formalization (Sec. 2.1) that distinguishes transductive transfer setting and black-box vs. grey-box access.
weaknesses: Limited model diversity undermines the model-bank ranking claim: all source models are 2D U-Nets trained by the authors (3 or 4 layer variants) on single datasets. Real model zoos contain heterogeneous architectures, training regimes, and normalization; the paper does not test whether CTE ranks across such diversity. The two BioImage Model Zoo models are used only as an add-on for cell segmentation without detailed analysis.

The model banks are very small (M_S = 3 to 7). With only 3-5 models, Kendall tau values of 1.00 (Mito, Std = 0.00 over 4 target datasets) are close to trivial and provide weak statistical evidence; no significance testing, confidence intervals, or discussion of the number of rankable pairs is provided.

A potential confound is not analyzed: a model that under-segments (predicts near-empty masks) will appear highly 'consistent' under perturbation. The foreground-union restriction mitigates but does not eliminate this; failure-mode models (e.g., transferring across large domain gaps) should be examined explicitly.

The same augmentations are used for training and for test-time perturbation, creating a possible circularity; there is no ablation over perturbation types or mismatched perturbations to show the estimator is not simply measuring augmentation-specific invariance.

Novelty is incremental: the core idea extends Effective Invariance (Deng et al.) from classification to segmentation, plus a Hamming/IoU-based 'hard' variant and a Rand-score variant. This is a reasonable adaptation but the methodological contribution is thin, and the paper lacks theoretical grounding for why consistency should correlate with zero-shot transfer performance in segmentation.

No comparison against other unsupervised baseline estimators (e.g., entropy-based confidence measures, agreement-rate baselines); the only baseline is a supervised method that the paper itself argues is mismatched.

Notation in Eq. (5) is ambiguous/incorrect as written (an inequality appears to be intersected with a set union), which hampers reproducibility; no code release or reproducibility statement is mentioned.

Instance segmentation results have large variance (Kendall tau std 0.23-0.26), and results rely on a single perturbation run; the claimed reliability for model selection would benefit from more careful statistical treatment.
Generality beyond microscopy (natural images, other architectures, foundation models) is untested, and there is no limitations discussion.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and under-explored problem: unsupervised (zero-shot) transferability estimation for segmentation models, motivated by real model-zoo workflows in microscopy; instance segmentation transferability estimation is indeed largely unaddressed in the literature.

The proposed estimator (CTE) is simple, computationally lightweight (two inference runs), and works for both black-box (input perturbation) and grey-box (feature/dropout perturbation) models, which suits the stated model-bank use case.

The paper introduces both a 'hard' (NHD/Rand-score-based) and a 'soft' (EI-based) consistency measure and reports that the hard variant is more robust, with a plausible explanation via calibration degradation under shift.

Experiments span multiple tasks (semantic mitochondria, semantic/instance nuclei, instance cells) and several public datasets, and the paper compares feature vs. input perturbations and sweeps perturbation strength, which supports robustness of the ranking to hyperparameters.
Reproducibility is helped by use of public datasets and publicly available pre-trained models from the BioImage Model Zoo.
weaknesses: The evidence base for the central claims is thin: model banks are very small (M_S = 3–5 for most settings, up to 7). A Kendall tau of 1.00 over 3 source models (Table 1, Mito) is nearly trivial to achieve and carries little statistical weight; no confidence intervals, significance tests, or ranking-stability analyses are provided for such small N, despite the authors reporting standard deviations that vary substantially across targets.

The claimed 'new state-of-the-art' is not convincingly established: the only baseline is CCFV, which is designed for supervised, fine-tuning transferability estimation, and the authors themselves acknowledge this mismatch. No other transferability estimators (e.g., LEEP, LogME variants, or unsupervised baselines adapted to segmentation) are compared, so it is unclear whether consistency under perturbation is genuinely superior or simply the only method tried.

Source-model diversity is limited: all source models are 2D U-Nets of similar architecture trained by the authors, which likely makes ranking easier and does not test the estimator in the realistic model-zoo scenario of heterogeneous architectures and training regimes; the two public zoo models are evaluated only anecdotally, without quantified results.

The method is a fairly direct extension of Effective Invariance [7] and consistency/uncertainty ideas from classification to segmentation. The technical novelty is incremental: the main additions are the NHD metric (essentially IoU between predictions) and foreground-restricted Rand scoring, both of which are standard segmentation measures applied between perturbed runs.

Several methodological choices are under-justified: the dropout layer choice ('bottleneck after encoder'), the foreground-union restriction in Eq. 3, and the median aggregation are stated without ablation; Eq. 5's notation is ambiguous (the intersection/union of a single pixel predicate with mask unions is unclear as written); and why a single perturbation run suffices is asserted rather than analysed, despite the known variance of dropout-based estimates.

The evaluation is confined to microscopy with a narrow modality range (fluorescence and EM) and 2D patches from 3D volumes; generalisation of the claim beyond this domain is not tested, yet the discussion overreaches in calling the approach a general state-of-the-art for segmentation transferability.

There is no limitations discussion and no analysis of failure cases (e.g., when perturbation strength is mis-set for a new domain, or when models are miscalibrated), even though the authors note that very strong perturbations degrade the ranking; guidance for practitioners on choosing θ or p in practice is missing.

Figures 2 and 3 are hard to read at the reported scale, and the reported correlations appear to be computed per target dataset and then averaged, which masks the per-target variability visible in the scatter plots (e.g., nuclei instance results with std of 0.23–0.26 for Kendall tau).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored problem: unsupervised (label-free) estimation of zero-shot transferability for segmentation models. The authors correctly point out that instance segmentation transferability estimation has not been addressed even in the supervised setting, making this a clear gap contribution.

The proposed method is practical and lightweight: requiring only two inference runs (one perturbed, one unperturbed), no access to source training data or target labels, and applicable to both black-box and grey-box models. This is well-matched to the motivating use case of model zoos and model banks in microscopy.

The evaluation is reasonably broad in terms of biological diversity: mitochondria segmentation in EM, nuclei instance/semantic segmentation, and cell instance segmentation, spanning ~15 public datasets, with correlation between the estimator and true performance assessed via Kendall tau, Spearman, and Pearson coefficients.

The comparison against CCFV (a supervised state-of-the-art) is informative: the unsupervised estimator outperforming a supervised baseline that also targets a different setting (fine-tuned transferability) is a notable, if partly incidental, result.

The paper includes useful ablations: perturbation strength sweeps (Fig. 3) showing ranking robustness across dropout rates, feature vs. input perturbation comparison, and soft (EI) vs. hard (NHD) consistency metrics, with plausible explanations for observed differences (calibration degradation under transfer).

The problem definition (Section 2.1) is clearly stated, including the transductive transfer assumption and the black-box/grey-box distinction, and the connection to consistency-based generalization metrics, UDA, and post-hoc uncertainty estimation is well motivated.
weaknesses: The scale of the model banks is very small (M_S = 3 to 7 models). Kendall tau of 1.00 with only 3 models has high sampling variance, and the reported standard deviations (e.g., 0.00 for Mito) suggest near-degenerate rank statistics. The statistical strength of 'strong correlation' claims is limited; significance testing or confidence intervals for the rank correlations are absent.

The source models are almost entirely self-trained 2D U-Nets with a shared training recipe (same loss, augmentations, architecture family). This narrows the diversity of the model bank relative to real-world model zoos (where architectures, training regimes, and data vary widely), and may inflate the observed correlation between consistency and performance. The two publicly available Zoo models are only added for cell segmentation. This limitation deserves explicit discussion but is not addressed.

The black-box variant of the method performs substantially worse than the grey-box variant (e.g., Cells instance: Kτ = 0.54 vs 0.87; Nuclei semantic input: Kτ = 0.73 vs 0.83). Since black-box applicability is one of the claimed advantages, the weaker input-perturbation results weaken the practical claim and merit deeper analysis.

Some technical presentation is imprecise or potentially incorrect: Eq. (5) writes the NHD numerator as an intersection between an event P(ŷp ≠ ŷ) and a set (ŷp ∪ ŷ), which is not well-formed as stated; the claimed 'equivalence to IoU' is asserted rather than derived; Eq. (3) refers to N_pix without defining how the foreground-union restriction interacts with normalization; and it is unclear how the Rand-score-based consistency (Eq. 6) applies when comparing a prediction to itself under perturbation rather than to ground truth.

The CCFV comparison is potentially unfair and under-analyzed: CCFV was designed to estimate fine-tuned (supervised) transferability, and the paper acknowledges this, yet frames the result as outperforming a state-of-the-art baseline. A more careful framing or an adapted baseline would strengthen the claim of 'new state-of-the-art'.

No failure-case analysis or conditions under which the estimator breaks down are provided (beyond extreme perturbation strength), e.g., models with systematically biased but consistent predictions, or domain shifts that affect calibration. There is also no theoretical justification for why consistency under dropout should rank transferability, only an appeal to related literature.

The evaluation reports results from a single pair of perturbed/unperturbed runs and claims averaging over multiple runs gave no advantage, but no variance estimates supporting this claim are shown. Reproducibility is also not supported: no mention of code or configuration release.

The manuscript is short and reads like a workshop/short paper; the experiments section would benefit from more thorough analysis (per-target-dataset breakdowns beyond averages, effect of dataset size n_T on estimator reliability, computational cost measurements).

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant gap: unsupervised, source-free model selection for segmentation, particularly pressing in biomedical imaging where annotation is costly and model repositories (e.g., BioImage Model Zoo) are growing. The problem framing — no target labels, no source data — matches realistic practitioner constraints.

First transferability estimator applicable to instance segmentation, where output-space non-correspondence makes classification-derived metrics inapplicable; the Adapted Rand Score formulation over perturbed vs. unperturbed predictions is a sensible and simple solution.

Extensive experimental evidence across many datasets (EM mitochondria, LM nuclei/cells, 3D multi-class CBCT ToothFairy2), model architectures (U-Nets, transformers, state space models, generalist models like µSAM and Cellpose-SAM), and perturbation types, with comprehensive ablations (perturbation strength sweeps) in the supplementary material showing robustness of the estimator.

Thorough baseline comparison against eight supervised transferability metrics and the SOTA unsupervised validation method (Transfer Score), including a well-designed auxiliary classification task to disentangle whether failures of classification-based metrics stem from domain shift or from the semantic segmentation setting itself. The analysis of why LEEP behaves differently is insightful.

Practical evaluation beyond synthetic transfer setups: reproducing ToothFairy2 challenge ranking without ground truth, and post-UDA model validation against Mean Teacher and AdaBN, demonstrate real-world applicability. The method needs only two inference passes per image, which is efficient.

Honest and substantive limitations discussion: mode collapse yielding spuriously high consistency, task-alignment assumptions violated by generalist models, and inapplicability to boundary-sensitive metrics. Supplementary analyses (e.g., cells-vs-nuclei mode switching) probe these failure modes empirically.

No contribution type is declared; the paper is best treated as Algorithms/General with strong Applied/Systems components, and the evidence (breadth of tasks, challenge reproduction, UDA validation) is appropriate to that type.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is a combination of existing ingredients (Effective Invariance, Rand Index/Adapted Rand Score, test-time dropout), adapted from classification/generalisation work to segmentation. The theoretical grounding is largely intuitive (margin/decision-boundary argument) without formal analysis of when consistency should correlate with transfer performance.

The mode-collapse failure mode is significant for the core use case: the worst models (degenerate all-background/all-foreground predictions) can receive artificially high consistency scores and be mis-ranked high. For a model-selection tool this is a consequential weakness; the suggested fix (pairing consistency with entropy/diversity) is only discussed, not implemented or evaluated.

Some statistical fragility: instance segmentation model pools are very small (|M|=5), making rank correlations barely meaningful; several correlations in supplementary tables are non-significant (e.g., DSB2018 Pearson near zero or negative in Tab. 18; VNC post-UDA results are weak for both CTE and TS). The 'strong correlation for all targets' claims in Sec. 5.2 rely on averaging over few and variable-per-target results.

The claim of 'state-of-the-art results' is somewhat overstated: in Table 1, supervised LEEP clearly outperforms all CTE variants on Mito (Kτ 0.89 vs 0.77, Sρ 0.96 vs 0.85), so the method is SOTA only within the unsupervised setting; this should be stated more carefully. Also no comparison against simpler unsupervised alternatives (e.g., prediction entropy, ensemble disagreement across multiple TTAs) as sanity baselines.

Several design choices are heuristic and not fully justified (median aggregation, per-class weighted averaging, single perturbation run per image, 'tolerable' perturbation range determined empirically); guidance for practitioners on selecting perturbation strength without labels is not provided, which limits out-of-the-box reproducibility of the reported performance.

Evaluation is confined to the biomedical domain; generalisation of the claims to natural-image segmentation (where CCFV and classification-derived metrics were originally validated) is asserted but not tested, weakening the breadth of the contribution's impact.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important problem: unsupervised, source-free ranking of semantic and instance segmentation models, which is highly relevant to the biomedical imaging community (e.g., BioImage Model Zoo, challenge models).

To my knowledge, this is the first transferability estimator for instance segmentation, enabled by operating in the output/prediction space (IoU/NHD, Rand-based ARS) rather than feature space — a sensible and well-motivated design choice that also sidesteps architecture-dependent feature geometries.

The empirical finding that classification-derived transferability metrics (LogME, NCTI, H-score, GBC, etc.), even supervised ones, fail to correlate with segmentation performance on biomedical data is itself a valuable negative result, and the auxiliary patch-classification experiments (Fig. 2) provide a clean ablation isolating domain shift from task formulation.

Broad and credible evaluation: 6 tasks, multiple modalities (EM, LM, CBCT), diverse architectures including recent models (UNETR, UMamba, VMamba, Cellpose-SAM, µSAM), reproduction of the ToothFairy2 challenge ranking, and post-UDA validation against the Transfer Score baseline.

Extensive supplementary material with perturbation-strength sweeps demonstrating robustness of the estimator to hyperparameter choices, and a candid limitations section (mode collapse, task alignment for generalist models, misalignment with boundary-sensitive metrics).
weaknesses: The method is technically simple: it is essentially Effective Invariance (EI) [15] extended to segmentation plus a Rand-index-based consistency variant for instances. The conceptual novelty is moderate; the paper's contribution rests largely on empirical validation rather than algorithmic or theoretical depth.

The acknowledged mode-collapse failure mode (degenerate constant predictions yield artificially high consistency) is a substantive limitation, and the proposed mitigation (pairing consistency with prediction diversity/entropy) is only sketched, not implemented or evaluated. This affects precisely the low-performing models that model selection most needs to weed out.

Model banks are small (|M| = 5–15), so rank correlations (Kendall tau, Spearman) are estimated from few points; statistical significance is reported for some tables, but the practical reliability of the ranking with small candidate sets remains uncertain. The high-variance instance segmentation results (e.g., σ = 0.21–0.28 on nuclei, several non-significant correlations in Tabs. 28–32) undermine the claim of a 'strong correlation' in that setting.

There are no unsupervised baselines for instance segmentation, so the instance results are essentially self-validated; for semantic segmentation the comparison against TS [78] is useful, but the supervised baselines are applied in settings outside their intended design (zero-shot, no fine-tuning assumptions), which slightly weakens the strength of the negative-result claims.

Experiments are confined to biomedical microscopy/CBCT data with same-task transfers. It is unclear whether CTE generalizes to natural-image segmentation or to cross-task settings; the transductive assumption (all target data available) also limits applicability and is not deeply discussed.
The claim of reproducibility rests on a promise that code will be made publicly available; no code or repository is actually provided with the submission.

strengths: Clear and practically important problem: unsupervised, source-free model selection for biomedical segmentation, a setting with no prior work for instance segmentation and limited options for semantic segmentation.

The proposed CTE is simple, model-agnostic (blackbox via input perturbations, greybox via dropout), requires only two inference passes per image, and operates in output space so it can compare models with heterogeneous architectures and instantiation strategies.

First transferability estimator for instance segmentation, enabled by the Rand/Adapted-Rand formulation that sidesteps the permutation/variable-length issues of instance outputs; this is a genuine technical contribution.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: six tasks (EM mitochondria, LM nuclei and cells, 42-class 3D CBCT ToothFairy2), dozens of models from small U-Nets to generalist models (µSAM, Cellpose-SAM, BioImage Model Zoo), challenge models, UDA settings (Mean Teacher, AdaBN), and extensive perturbation-strength sweeps in the supplementary showing stability.

Honest failure-mode analysis: mode-collapse cases yielding spuriously high consistency, task-mismatch issues for generalist models (Figs. 5-6), the weak VNC results and their explanations are reported transparently; limitations section is substantive.

Insightful analysis of why existing supervised metrics (and even LEEP/NLEEP) behave differently in segmentation vs classification, including the clean disentangling experiment with a patch-classification auxiliary task.
The ToothFairy2 experiment reproduces a real challenge ranking without ground truth, which is a compelling practical demonstration.
weaknesses: The method is largely heuristic: the connection between perturbation consistency and transferability is motivated intuitively (margin/proxy arguments) but no theory or guarantees are given, and the choice among CTE-EI/CTE-NHD/CTE-ARS or among perturbation types is settled purely empirically, with occasional inconsistencies (e.g., CTE-NHD Pearson unstable for nuclei in Tab. 18 while Kτ remains high; different perturbation variants win in different settings, leaving no single recommended configuration clearly justified).

Evaluation is confined to biomedical microscopy/CBCT with relatively small model banks per experiment (|M|=5-15); correlation estimates on 5-7 models have wide confidence intervals (many supplementary tables show non-significant correlations, e.g., instance segmentation results where only Pearson is significant), so the strength of the headline claims is overstated in places.

Moderate correlations in several settings: instance segmentation mean Kτ ≈0.69-0.80, post-UDA VNC fails (Kτ 0.21-0.39, n.s.), and some ToothFairy2 per-structure results are weak (Sinus Kτ 0.43 n.s.); the approach is a ranking heuristic rather than a reliable predictor in all regimes.

Known failure modes are acknowledged but not solved: mode collapse produces artificially high consistency, and generalist models can switch segmentation 'modes' without affecting consistency; the suggested fixes (pairing with entropy/diversity, pixel-importance weighting) are left to future work, so a practitioner applying the method cannot detect when it will fail.

Comparison to the single unsupervised baseline (Transfer Score) is somewhat narrow; no comparison against simpler cheap alternatives (e.g., ensembles over test-time augmentations, entropy-based scores) that a practitioner might try.
Code is only promised, not available at review time, which limits reproducibility verification of the large experimental grid.

Some writing/presentation issues: inconsistent notation and naming of datasets across main paper and supplementary, dense table-heavy supplementary that makes it hard to extract overall conclusions, and a few claims (e.g., 'state-of-the-art results') that are not backed by a formal benchmark since baselines for instance segmentation do not exist.
